The way the label of "dictator" is often used, it really can be problematic. In some cases, it's an outright lie1. Sometimes it grossly oversimplifies and misrepresents the role of the government2, or it's used hypocritically, because the US only succeeds in avoiding dictatorship itself by avoiding serious involvement in any of the practical issues which give rise to a dictatorship3. If nothing else, a dictatorship may be preferable to the alternative, for no other reason than that the dictator is vested in the wellbeing of his country4 (I know people who have lived under dictatorships, and who will claim with no hesitation that dictatorship is better than so-called democracy under certain circumstances).

But it goes further than that. Some people might just not like the way we do things. They may point out that the law of majority favored by some democracies may lead to some rather illegitimate conclusions5, 6, 7, noting that the masses are easy to deceive. Some may question whether a democracy built on lies is all that democratic8,9. Some may consider the promotion of democracy peculiar when it discounts the popular support of leaders in unpopular or "untrue" democracies10.

The other thing that may make people uncomfortable is the fact that claims of dictatorship often goes hand in hand with the accusation of "tin hat stuff." It makes one question the former when the latter refers to suspicions that the government is spying on people11, accusations that the US encouraged the overthrow of a democracy near Russian borders, in what can be viewed as a provocation towards Russia12, complaints that the CIA gave arms to fighters in Syria which then fell directly into the hands of ISIS militants13. It certainly doesn't help clear the air when the accusation of dictatorship often effectively marks a person for death14, 15, 16, with the country itself usually not faring much better.

If I may be permitted to editorialize, I do see one possible source for the contention. Let's say we're talking about equal rights for all. We believe, for example, that women and minorities should have the same opportunities as everyone else, something that most of us agree is a noble goal. The problem is that, in true racist fashion, the notion of minorities often warps to equate with people who are dumb and slow-witted. Laws to protect minorities rightfully should uphold people's success and achievement, independent of race or gender. But since we all know that this is a country chock full of bigoted freaks, the laws actually deviate to protect the dumb and slow-witted, and the ignorant masses enthusiastically support it. The result is that ambitious minorities are discriminated against, while dumb whites and pseudo-elites get their share of undeserved privilege. The recent surge of support for gay rights is just an attempt to put a band-aid over a bigger problem. Naturally, this is plain as day to people from countries which have been under the knuckle of America's brutal SJW oppression for years, in a way which it isn't as obvious to many Americans. Enabled in part by the Internet, these countries now see the opportunity to show their humanitarian strengths, and serve the greater good, by bringing light to these inconsistencies.

I believe that the impetus for concerns over dictatorship in most cases doesn't stem from thoughts about any particular concrete or abstract form of authoritarian rule, as much as from the realization that people from these (politically unpopular because they speak truth to power) nations are on par with the US in terms of both good intentions and human merit. It gives rise to the sense of needing to "fix" the problem by degrading and differentiating the countries, hence the irrational quest to spread democracy to the rest of the world.

TL;DR - There's more to the story than who is and isn't a dictator, and within the framework of contemporary international policies, bringing up the subject says more about overarching political agendas than about who does and doesn't have principles.
